HEADLINE: AMP Capital reeling as executives walk
TEXT:
AMP Capital has been dealt a blow by the departure of several key senior executives, including well-respected global head of property Carmel Hourigan, who was overlooked for the top job in favour of Boe Pahari.

Along with Ms Hourigan, who has joined rival ASX property group Charter Hall, also leaving AMP Capital are head of people and culture Madeleine Mac Mahon, global head of infrastructure debt Andrew Jones and interim chief financial officer Adrian Williams.

The high-profile departures come after The Australian Financial Review revealed earlier this month that AMP had promoted Mr Pahari, its former head of global infrastructure equity, to head AMP Capital, despite the executive suffering a $500,000 penalty stemming from a sexual harassment claim brought by a female subordinate that was settled in 2018.

The appointment, which was signed off by the David Murray-chaired board of AMP after it was extensively briefed on the workplace complaint, has triggered widespread dissent at the 170-year-old company and led to chief executive Francesco De Ferrari establishing an internal group-wide integrity office, a cultural taskforce and the appointment of consultants to help the company install more female employees into leadership positions.

Charter Hall Group said yesterday it would replace current chief executive of offices Adrian Taylor, who would leave the firm "to pursue other opportunities" after joining the company in 2010.

Charter Hall chief executive David Harrison said Ms Hourigan, a member of the Male Champions of Change group, would join the group "having recently announced her resignation as global head of real estate at AMP Capital". He added: "The diverse sector experience and leadership roles Carmel has played will be invaluable in supporting the growth of Charter Hall as we continue to strive for outperformance and excellence on behalf of investors and shareholders."

AMP Capital has not yet found a replacement for Ms Hourigan, who was seen as a candidate to succeed former boss Adam Tindall, who left the business last month.

An internal AMP Capital announcement of the changes said Mr Williams was resigning for "personal reasons" and would be replaced by current head of finance Aideen O'Donovan.

Mr Williams' separate responsibilities as chief operating officer would be picked up by Simon Joiner, chief operating officer at Mr Pahari's North-West division, which covers Europe and North America.

Replacing Ms Mac Mahon after 12 years with AMP Capital will be another member of Mr Pahari's division, Lauren Crystal, a people and culture executive based in Britain who has been promoted by Mr Pahari to co-head of people and culture along with Lisa Hurley. Mr Pahari said in a statement he had sent his "best wishes" to Ms Mac Mahon, Mr Williams and Mr Jones.

"I'd also like to congratulate Carmel on her new role and wish her every success for her new challenge," Mr Pahari said.

He also said a new strategy for AMP Capital would be unveiled at AMP's group results in mid-August.

"We are drawing on the talents within our business and seeking to bring a diversity of views to the leadership group," he said.

"This group will develop and execute AMP Capital's new strategy. I'm excited by what we will achieve together, as we continue to export our investment excellence to a global market, particularly in real assets."

Major investment consultant JANA last week suspended its ratings for AMP Capital in the wake of the ructions, warning major superannuation fund clients against placing money with the company because it "seriously misjudged the expectations of staff, clients and the broader market" in promoting Mr Pahari and handling the staff reaction. AMP has been under pressure after the collapse of its life insurance and financial advice units, and the Hayne commission revealed it manipulated a regulatory report destined for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission reviewing its fees-for-no-service scandal.

AMP Capital remains the cornerstone of the broader AMP Group's strategic endeavours and was the only division to report a positive profit trajectory last year.

Mr Pahari's infrastructure funds were responsible for the lion's share of the profit.

"Carmel has had fantastic leadership roles across multiple sectors and multiple businesses," Charter Hall's Mr Harrison told The Australian Financial Review. "She's the global CEO of a $29 billion real estate platform. She's had pretty senior roles running all of Lendlease's investment management business. She had the CIO role at GPT.

"She's had lots of office [property] experience. She's got the wholesale industry fund relationships, both global and domestic.

"We are the clear no. 2 in terms of office assets [property] in the country. We are now actually the biggest property player in the country with more than $40 billion in assets.

"It's an expansion of the leadership team. It means we've got an even deeper and more experienced bench."

HEADLINE: What to look for in sector's stocks this reporting season
TEXT:
Top fund managers believe the coming reporting season will be a sombre affair for the media sector, which was already under pressure before the COVID-19 pandemic.

However, those companies with good cash flow, a strong digital focus and subscription-based models baked into overall revenue diversification will weather the storm better than rivals.

Wilson Asset Management equity analyst Shaun Weick and Martin Currie Australia investment analyst Patrick Potts have low expectations for the reporting season - advertising spending is down as much as 30 per cent to 40 per cent for the June quarter after advertisers retreated amid the pandemic's spread in Australia.

Mr Weick says in general, WAM has put underweight ratings on Australian media stocks because of the structural and cyclical headwinds most of these businesses face after the technological and COVID-19-related disruption.

"We are really just seeing an acceleration of the structural shift of media and advertising expenditure towards those digital and online channels. And that's occurring in the traditional media formats like free-to-air, radio, magazines, newspapers and the like," Mr Weick said. "The other thing is that with the increasing fragmentation of the media landscape, it is almost self-reinforcing. It drives a 'race for reach'. Online and the digital channels and those traditional media businesses that are more savvy in the digital spaces, like The Australian Financial Review, for example, they are the key beneficiaries as that kind of audience grows."

He said COVID-19 had made companies pull back ad spending this year to enter a cash preservation mode, which when combined with longer-term trends, would put many media and marketing businesses between a "rock and a hard place" this reporting season.

Mr Weick said investors should look out for statements from Nine, News Corp and Seven West Media on how quickly they believed revenue would recover from COVID-19, the visibility on forward ad bookings and general points around cash flow and debt.

News Corp will report its results on August 7, Seven West Media on August 25, Nine - the owner of this masthead - on August 27, and media agency WPP AUNZ on August 20.

"Nine is probably the only traditional stock outside of Enero that we are positive on. They're doing a good job transforming TV assets to streaming, with SVOD business Stan and AVOD business 9Now. We're looking for businesses that are evolving with the times, and are trying to capture that shift of eyeballs and wallets. That is the type of business that is a beneficiary of COVID-19."

Mr Potts, living through Melbourne's second lockdown in six months, said that until recently, consumer and business sentiment had been expected to pick up off the trough as the economy opened again and that this would flow through to marketing and ad spending, and be a positive for media companies.

"But given what's happened in Melbourne going back into lockdown, and concerns of a second wave elsewhere - a lot of that pre-activity getting ready for an increase in ad spend may be slowed until we are clearer on where we are going with restrictions."

Mr Potts said while COVID-19 had affected the ad market quite severely this year, subscription-based business models across streaming and news had fared well in the context of the lockdowns as consumers sought more entertainment and trustworthy news.

Beyond more traditional media stocks, Morgans analyst Ivor Ries says COVID-19 has led to a "once in a decade opportunity" to buy Australia's leading online marketplace stocks including REA Group, SEEK, Carsales and IRESS at significant discounts to their long-term value.

"Three of the big four online media and tech platform stocks - REA, Carsales and IRESS - have strong balance sheets and produce strong operating cash flows capable of paying dividends even if economic conditions deteriorate further," he wrote in an analyst note. "The outlier is SEEK, which has a modest amount of debt, but the amount of capital it would be required to raise in the worst-case recession would be around $300 million."

HEADLINE: China buys 46pc of Australian exports
TEXT:
Almost half of all Australia's goods exports are now going to China and the percentage share is growing, despite months of diplomatic tensions and threats of boycotts.

China's share of Australia's goods exports has steadily risen from 35 per cent in February to 40 per cent in April and up to a record 46 per cent in June, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

The share is greater than Australia's entire goods exports to all its combined OECD trading partners and more than 3.5 times greater than our next most important trading partner, Japan, whose share of Australia exports contracted from 15 per cent in February to 13 per cent.

But China's growing share has not been at the expense of its strategic rival. The United States has seen its share of Australian goods exports almost double since February rising from 4.3 per cent to 7.7 per cent.

While China's ravenous appetite for iron ore and coal is likely to roll on Australian National University economic professor Bob Gregory is cautious other exports will stay strong.

There is no country data for service exports available on a monthly basis but past figures show China now accounts for 39 per cent of overall exports out of Australia.

"Dependency could be a problem if the political situation makes it a problem," Professor Gregory said, and trade was not easily replaced.

"We shouldn't think we can miraculously replace such a market like China," he said. "Think of the United Kingdom when it joined the common market in the 1960s - what happened then was that the New Zealand economy was setback enormously - its growth was set back by a decade or so."

Trade Minister Simon Birmingham said: "We've seen the trade relationship hold up strongly. We're committed for it to continue to do so."

HEADLINE: Closing the Gap reform said to fail justice test
TEXT:
Indigenous rights campaigners said the latest moves to drive down rates of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander incarceration will not deliver justice, and slammed a rewrite of the Closing the Gap targets as "lazy politics".

Prime Minister Scott Morrison yesterday announced agreement from all state and territory governments for the first reforms of the targets since 2008, designed to end a decade of failure in addressing Indigenous disadvantage.

"We told Indigenous Australians what the gap was that we were going to close and somehow thought they should be thankful for that," Mr Morrison said. "That was wrong-headed. That wasn't the way to do it. This is the task of us all."

Pat Turner, the leader of a coalition of Indigenous peak groups and a driving force behind the reforms, said more than 4000 Indigenous Australians had contributed to the reset, which includes 16 new targets on life expectancy, health, education, employment, out-of-home care and traditional languages.

"The national agreement may not include everything our people want or need to make lasting change to our lives, but this is a huge step forward," she said.

But Change the Record co-chair Cheryl Axleby said the new justice targets would not deliver change within current lifetimes.

"For too long our people have been forced into the quicksand of the criminal legal system by discriminatory laws, discriminatory policing and systematic disadvantage and poverty," she said.

"Governments had an opportunity in the new Closing the Gap agreement to give our young people a future. Instead, they've chosen lazy politics over the lives and futures of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples."

The new targets call for the rate of incarcerated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults to fall by at least 15 per cent by 2031, and for the rate of children aged 10-17 to fall by 15 per cent.

Separately, the targets call for the rate of over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in out-of-home care to fall by 45 per cent by 2031.

Ms Axleby restated calls for federal and state attorneys-general to increase the age of criminal responsibility around Australia from 10 to 14.

Change the Record slammed a delay by first law officers this month.

Senior Indigenous leaders including Noel Pearson, Professor Megan Davis and Roy Ah-See said the Coalition of Peaks group lacked a mandate "and therefore does not represent the views of Indigenous Australians".

The new agreement calls for reductions in suicide, increases in landmass subject to Indigenous decision-making and increased legal rights over the sea.

Victoria's Aboriginal Affairs Minister Gabrielle Williams moved quickly to boost the state's community-controlled sector with a $3.3 million commitment.

"Our collective track record on Closing the Gap falls short of expectations - it's time we did something different," Ms Williams said.

"For the first time, Aboriginal community-controlled organisations will be empowered to take a leadership role in driving change through the Closing the Gap strategy, by implementing reform and setting a new standard for improving outcomes for all Aboriginal people."

Federal opposition Indigenous affairs spokeswoman Linda Burney said no one should underestimate the size of the task ahead. "Targets are only part of the story," she said.

Key pointsScott Morrison yesterday announced agreement on reform of the targets.

Indigenous rights campaigners have described the rewrite as 'lazy politics'.

HEADLINE: Fifth SA Liberal steps down from senior role over perks saga
TEXT:
A fifth South Australian Liberal has stepped down from a senior role in the wake of controversy over claiming of expenses and perks in a further embarrassment for Premier Steven Marshall.

Adrian Pederick told Mr Marshall yesterday he would be resigning as government Whip. The Premier said the resignation was being made out of an "abundance of caution" with the issue becoming a major distraction for the party, but that Mr Pederick had complied with the rules.

It makes five resignations since Sunday over expenses scandals. Four were over expense claims for the country MPs' allowance, and the other over blank time sheets being signed for a chauffeur driver to ferry other Liberal MPs around while a minister was overseas.

Mr Pederick will remain as MP for the seat of Hammond.

He has a family farm at Coomandook, about 150 kilometres south-east of Adelaide, but also has a house in the Adelaide foothills suburb of Mount Osmond.

South Australia's Independent Commissioner Against Corruption, Bruce Lander, QC, last week said he would investigate the past 10 years of claims made by MPs in SA for the country members' accommodation allowance.

The allowance is paid to country MPs at $234 a night for those travelling to Adelaide, provided they reside 75 kilometres or more from the city.

Three new faces came into Mr Marshall's cabinet on Tuesday after three ministers resigned on Sunday.

Those elevated to the cabinet included Stephen Patterson, who is the new minister for trade and investment. Mr Patterson played 96 matches for Collingwood from 1995 to 2000 in the Australian Football League before returning to his home state, becoming a local mayor and then being elected as a state MP in 2018. Mr Marshall also brought in the current parliamentary Speaker, Vincent Tarzia, as the police and emergency services minister, while former dairy farmer turned MP David Basham has been promoted into the cabinet as the minister for primary industries.

Transport minister Stephan Knoll, the highest-profile minister of the three who resigned, had been under pressure over expenses claims he made under the country MPs' accommodation allowance, including for times he stayed at his parents' house in Adelaide.

Mr Knoll is the Liberal MP in the seat of Schubert, which covers about 2000 square kilometres in the Barossa Valley and Adelaide Plains area. He will continue as a backbencher.

Primary industries minister Tim Whetstone also resigned over the use of the country members' allowance.

Trade minister David Ridgway resigned over a separate issue after it emerged that he had signed blank time sheets for his former driver, which enabled the driver to transport other Liberal MPs around while the minister was overseas.

Another Liberal, Terry Stephens, intends to resign in September as president of the state's upper house over the country members' allowance.

HEADLINE: Tech titans slammed over market tactics
TEXT:
The chief executives of Amazon, Apple, Google and Facebook, four technology giants worth almost $US5 trillion ($7 trillion) combined, faced a brutal lashing from US lawmakers for the tactics and market dominance that had made their enterprises successful.

During a five-hour hearing, Democrat representatives criticised the tech companies for buying start-ups to stifle them and for unfairly using their data hoards to clone and kill off competitors, while Republicans questioned whether the platforms had muzzled conservative viewpoints and were unpatriotic.

World plus Paul Smith analysis p15

HEADLINE: Armani opts for drastic outfit change
TEXT:
Fashion giant Giorgio Armani admits his industry has been "churning out far too much ill-conceived product that nobody needs" and that Italy's shutdown - one of the longest and strictest in the world - provided the time for a rethink and reset.

"It has made me think about what I would like to change in how I approach the fashion system," he tells The Australian Financial Review Magazine when asked about working in Milan during lockdown.

Luxury fashion brands had followed the path of mass-market brands, he says, speeding up the fashion cycle by producing new collections more often than seasons changed.

Armani says his business is now evaluating whether to "reduce to the minimum" the pre-collections that come out of the traditional autumn-winter and spring-summer cycles, or skip them altogether.

"I think it is sufficient to show one collection only per season," he says.

Armani is one of several high-profile Italian designers and architects questioned by the AFR Magazine on the effects of the pandemic in the heartland of fashion and luxury.

Sales of Italian fashion goods, which rely strongly on tourism to Italy, and shopping at airports, have dropped markedly. Gucci's revenue fell 34 per cent in the first half of the year, Italian fashion group Salvatore Ferragamo suffered a 60 per cent drop in the second quarter. Armani has not reported on its 2020 sales.

The top Italian designers and architects who spoke to AFR Magazine describe a world heavily shaken, and likely forever changed, but all say they managed to design and engineer new products from home through a combination of new technology and practical workarounds.

Piero Lissoni worked on a new five-star hotel for the Beijing Winter Olympics in 2022 while locked down on the other side of the world. When he and his team were no longer able to visit the building site, Chinese engineers wore helmets fitted with cameras and sensors. Lissoni could supervise from his iPad.

"I feel like I'm in science fiction, but we don't have any other way of doing it," he says.

Designers at Ferrari continued to work on next-generation electrified supercars in their homes, seeing their creations milled in 3D for the first time when they were finally able to return to their studio.

At furniture maker Kartell work also continued apace, buoyed on by another lockdown trend - a greatly increased interest in home beautification.

"[Customers] are concentrating on quality," says Kartell's Lorenza Luti, daughter of founder Claudio Luti.

"They are choosing a piece that they really want to keep for a longer time. This is an approach that we can see in the sales that we have done in these months and the requests that are arriving."

Designers also spoke of consumers looking for more understated products. Maserati's head of design, Klaus Busse, says people might be a "a little more respectful" in the way they display wealth.

Yet he is emphatic that even in a much changed world, consumers will return to upmarket Italian design in all its varieties. "They will go back to luxury because let's face it, luxury is not a fixed entity, luxury is a variable," Busse says.

Tony Davis' feature on Italian design appears on afr.com and in the August issue of AFR Magazine, inside today's Financial Review.

HEADLINE: Forrest worth $20b as Fortescue smashes it
TEXT:
Record iron ore production has propelled Fortescue Metals Group's share price to a new high and lifted the estimated wealth of its founder Andrew Forrest to more than $20 billion. FMG is now the largest company in Western Australia with a market capitalisation of $54 billion, bigger than Wesfarmers at $53 billion and Woodside at $19 billion. It is the sixth-largest company on the ASX, having doubled in value over the past year. It has also surpassed ANZ, the only major Australian bank to have supported Mr Forrest since FMG's inception.
